hints: A systematic error makes repeated readings consistently too high or too low.
Consider a fault in the analogue voltmeter that is present before any reading is taken.
walkthrough: A systematic error is a consistent bias, so it affects every measurement in a similar direction.
For an analogue voltmeter, a pointer that does not read zero when no potential difference is applied will offset every reading.
This zero error is therefore a valid example of a systematic error.

ai_rubric.observable: Describes a consistent voltmeter fault, such as a zero offset or incorrect calibration, that biases every reading.

hints: A random error makes individual readings vary unpredictably rather than shifting them all in one direction.
For an analogue scale, consider what can vary when a person judges the needle position or reads it from a viewing angle.
walkthrough: A random error causes a scatter in readings because its size or direction varies from one observation to another.
The apparent position of an analogue needle can change when the scale is viewed from different angles, producing a variable reading error.
Reading the scale from different angles is therefore a valid example of a random error.

ai_rubric.observable: Describes a variable analogue-scale reading error, such as parallax from changing viewing angle or inconsistent interpolation between divisions.

hints: The known potential difference and resistance can be used directly; choose the power relationship containing both quantities.
Use P = V² / R, then substitute 5.0 V and 125 Ω with the voltage squared before division.
walkthrough: Use the electrical-power relationship P = V² / R because the potential difference and resistance are given.
Substitute the values: P = (5.0 V)² / 125 Ω.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses P = V² / R, or combines P = VI with V = IR, for the resistor.
Evaluates the supplied values to obtain 0.20 W.

hints: First express the 0.1 V uncertainty as a percentage of the 5.0 V reading.
Power is proportional to V²/R, so the voltage percentage uncertainty contributes twice before the resistance percentage is added.
walkthrough: For P = V²/R, the squared voltage contributes twice its percentage uncertainty: 2 × 2% = 4%.
Add the 3% resistance uncertainty: percentage uncertainty in P = 4% + 3% = 7%.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the potential-difference percentage uncertainty as 2%, or gives the equivalent fraction 0.02.
Doubles the voltage contribution for V² and adds the 3% resistance uncertainty to obtain 7%.

hints: Use the 7% uncertainty from part (b)(ii) as a fraction of the unrounded 0.20 W power from part (b)(i).
After finding the absolute uncertainty, round it suitably and give the power to the same decimal place.
walkthrough: Convert the 7% uncertainty to a fraction: 7% = 0.07.
Apply it to the calculated power: ΔP = 0.07 × 0.20 W = 0.014 W.
Round the absolute uncertainty to one significant figure: ΔP = 0.01 W.
Quote the central value to the same decimal place: P = 0.20 ± 0.01 W.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses 7% of 0.20 W to obtain an unrounded absolute uncertainty of 0.014 W.
Reports the result as 0.20 ± 0.01 W, or an equivalent correctly rounded standard-form expression.
